The man in the suit sat behind four feet of mahogany desk. The dark brown hair and neatly trimmed beard only added to the corporate executive look. The unfocused brown eyes detracted only slightly from his apparent authority. The half smile on a face that looked like it never smiled enough was disturbing.

"Interesting," said the man in a small, still voice. "You think you shouldn't be here."

"Get out of my head."

"Unlikely. I am everywhere."

"So you want me to believe you're God and this is Heaven."

"The afterlife. And the before-life once you move on from here."

The visitor felt like scowling but, for some reason, couldn't.

"Let me help."

"I don't need…" the visitor began, only to pause as a fly-out window popped up somewhere beyond… sensing?

"Choose and avatar and things will become easier. You can change it later."

The visitor spoke distractedly. "This looks like something from a video game."

"Indeed. Folks coming from your realm bring many wonderful ideas."

The visitor resolved with a harrumph, taking on the form of a dark skinned, white haired woman.

"A change from your usual?" the man inquired.

The woman folded her arms and spoke, "So. Atheism is wrong."

"Oh, yes. There are gods. But you didn't follow any of their dogmas. If you had you would be in one of their zones and we wouldn't be having this conversation. For you things are unsorted. Therefore you must have access to the creative panels."

"That sounds kind of harsh. Wait. Zones?"

"Yes. Try not to get stuck in them or you might be there for a long time."

"Wait. So because I didn't follow a religion I get kicked out of," the woman paused, trying to gather her thoughts.

"No. In this realm you only leave when you choose to disconnect. The gods withhold the knowledge of that option."

The woman opened her mouth to ask another question but the man interrupted her, "Yes, you have been here before. No, you won't remember it because you can only access the Akashic Record, and your part in it, when between life and death. And it is time for you to go. Don't worry, you're clever. You'll figure out the controls quickly enough."

The world resolved into a small pseudo-hellenic plaza at the top of a grassy hill. Off in the distance there was a mishmash of buildings. Some looked like something you would find in any city. Others looked like the products of an outrageously untalented art colony stacked one on top of the other then painted with the goop from inside glowsticks.

The woman found a marble bench and sat. She though about what she had just experienced and could draw no conclusions.

And that fly-out window was still open. She began to fiddle with the settings.
